speaker: Feng Zhang
title: 323 - CRISPR and the future of gene editing with Feng Zhang
question: In ocular gene therapy for inherited retinal blindness, why do treatments typically restore only partial sight rather than full vision?
guest: I think it's in the retina. You know, the retina doesn't regenerate, so if it's already degenerating, you have to deal with what is left in the retina. And so what you can restore is really capped by whatever is already left there. Plus there are also inefficiencies in the delivery systems—you're not restoring a hundred percent of the cells. And if you're layering on gene editing on top of it, which also has less than a hundred percent efficiency, when you multiply that all together, that's why you're not getting full restoration. I think it's very hard to fully restore vision. If you really want to fully restore vision, you probably have to regenerate the retina, so you have to replenish cells that are missing.

points.core: Adult retinal tissue cannot regenerate, capping recovery at the surviving cells remaining.
points.note: Accept: photoreceptors or retinal cells do not regenerate once lost, so vision recovery is bounded by remaining viable cells at treatment time. Do not credit: blaming brain neuroplasticity alone or vague references to disease progression.

points.core: Sub-complete delivery efficiency compounds multiplicatively with imperfect intracellular gene editing efficiency.
points.note: Accept: viral or vector delivery reaches fewer than 100% of cells and editing succeeds in fewer than 100% of delivered cells, multiplying losses together. Do not credit: mentioning delivery issues vaguely without noting the compounding with editing efficiency.

points.core: Achieving full vision restoration requires actually replenishing the lost retinal cells.
points.note: Accept: regenerating the retina, replacing dead photoreceptors, or restoring lost cell populations rather than only repairing surviving cells. Do not credit: generic calls for earlier diagnosis or better vectors without mentioning cell replenishment.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Gene therapy can only rescue cells that are still alive, and by the time most patients are treated, many of their photoreceptors have already died. Therapies such as voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna, for RPE65-related disease) deliver a working gene copy that restores function in surviving retinal cells, but they cannot regenerate lost photoreceptors or rebuild degenerated retinal circuitry.

Several other factors compound this. The subretinal injection treats only the region of retina under the injected fluid bleb, and not every cell in that area takes up the vector, so coverage is incomplete. Expression levels from the delivered gene may fall short of normal physiological levels. In people with early-onset disease, the visual cortex never developed normally (amblyopia-like limits), so the brain cannot make full use of the improved retinal signals. Finally, degeneration often continues despite treatment, and surgery or inflammation can cause some damage, particularly to the fovea.

The result is typically meaningful gains in light sensitivity and low-light navigation, rather than restored sharp acuity. This is why earlier treatment, while more cells survive, generally gives better outcomes.

points.why: The response identifies permanent photoreceptor loss as the reason recovery is limited to cells still alive at treatment.
quotes: Gene therapy can only rescue cells that are still alive

points.why: The response describes incomplete vector uptake and reduced gene expression but gives no mechanism in which imperfect editing compounds delivery losses.
The response says current therapies cannot regenerate lost photoreceptors but does not state that full restoration requires replenishing them.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Ocular gene therapy typically restores partial rather than full vision because it rescues surviving tissue rather than rebuilding an intact visual system. Inherited retinal diseases destroy cells progressively before treatment, and gene replacement can only revive living, dormant photoreceptors or retinal pigment epithelium—it cannot regenerate dead neurons or undo secondary rewiring of inner retinal circuits. Delivery constraints further limit recovery: viral vectors reach only a localized retinal patch, transduce a fraction of target cells, and rarely replicate natural gene-expression levels, while already-stressed cells may continue degenerating. In advanced disease where photoreceptors are gone, optogenetic therapies make surviving inner neurons light-sensitive, but bypassing the retina's native signal-amplification and image-processing layers yields low acuity, reduced light sensitivity, and limited color or contrast perception. Finally, in congenital or early-onset blindness, prolonged deprivation during developmental critical periods restricts visual cortex maturation, limiting how sharply the brain can interpret newly restored signals.

points.why: The response explicitly ties recovery to surviving retinal cells because gene replacement cannot regenerate cells already lost.
quotes: gene replacement can only revive living, dormant photoreceptors or retinal pigment epithelium

points.why: The response describes incomplete vector delivery but omits the additional loss from imperfect editing within cells that receive the vector.
The response explains the limits of rescuing surviving cells without identifying replenishment of lost retinal cells as necessary for full restoration.

noweb.answer: Ocular gene therapy can rescue only cells that are still alive, and by the time most patients with inherited retinal blindness are treated, many photoreceptors and supporting pigment epithelium cells have already permanently degenerated without the capacity to regenerate. Even among surviving cells, viral delivery has physical limits: subretinal injections treat only a localized patch of the retina, intravitreal vectors poorly penetrate outer retinal layers, and transduced cells rarely express the therapeutic gene at uniform, native physiological levels. Moreover, pre-existing cellular stress, abnormal remodeling of downstream retinal circuits, and vector-triggered inflammation can continue to constrain function after gene replacement. Finally, sight depends on the brain as well as the eye; patients deprived of clear visual input during early developmental critical periods often lack mature wiring in their visual pathways and cortex, limiting sharp acuity and complex visual processing even when retinal light sensitivity substantially improves.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Gene therapy can only rescue retinal cells that are still alive. It adds a working copy of the faulty gene, as Luxturna does for RPE65, but it can't regrow photoreceptors that have already died. Most inherited retinal diseases are degenerative, so by the time patients are treated many rods and cones, especially in the central macula, are already lost. Whatever function they carried is gone for good.

Delivery is another limit. Subretinal injection of the AAV vector treats only the area covered by the injection bleb, so cells outside it stay untreated. Gene expression also varies from cell to cell and may not reach normal levels. Surgery itself can thin or detach the fovea, and immune or inflammatory reactions can reduce the benefit.

Degeneration may keep going after treatment too. Long-term follow-up of RPE65 trials found photoreceptors still being lost even though they had initially responded, and the gains faded over time. Finally, the retina and brain have usually adapted to years of poor input, for example through nystagmus and amblyopia, which limits recovery even where the cells work again. That's why treatment earlier in life tends to give better results.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Ocular gene therapy for inherited retinal blindness typically restores only partial sight because it can rescue surviving, dysfunctional cells but cannot regenerate photoreceptors that have already died. By the time most patients are treated, significant and irreversible retinal degeneration and neural remodeling have already occurred. In addition, current delivery methods have physical limits: subretinal injections usually treat only a localized patch of the retina, and viral vectors rarely transduce every target cell within that area. Even in successfully transduced cells, the introduced gene is driven by an artificial promoter that may not replicate the exact timing or expression levels of the native gene, while dosing is constrained by the risk of retinal inflammation and immune reactions. Finally, in congenital forms of blindness, early visual deprivation often impairs the development of the visual cortex and causes issues like nystagmus, limiting how sharply the brain can interpret newly restored retinal signals. As a result, patients commonly gain meaningful improvements in light sensitivity and navigation rather than full visual acuity.

points.why: The response explicitly ties partial recovery to the fact that therapy can rescue only surviving cells.
quotes: it can rescue surviving, dysfunctional cells but cannot regenerate photoreceptors that have already died

points.why: The response describes incomplete transduction and altered gene expression, leaving out the additional loss from unsuccessful editing in transduced cells.
The response identifies irreversible photoreceptor loss but leaves unstated that full restoration requires replenishing the lost cells.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Most ocular gene therapies can restore function only in surviving retinal cells that receive the treatment. By the time someone is treated, the disease may already have destroyed many of the light-sensing cells needed for vision, and adding a working copy of a gene cannot bring those cells back. Treatment also typically reaches only part of the retina, so the benefit depends on where enough viable cells remain.

Different aspects of sight depend on different cells and retinal regions. For example, a person may become much better at seeing in dim light and navigating a room while still having difficulty reading or recognizing faces. The degree of recovery depends on the specific disease, how far it has progressed, and which cells the therapy can reach.
